goals: Explain how a Daniell cell produces a current and write its half-reactions and cell notation
Describe the standard hydrogen electrode, its preparation, use and limitations
Explain how the standard electrode potentials of Zn²⁺/Zn and Cu²⁺/Cu are measured against the SHE

slides.heading: Electrochemical cells
slides.body_md: Part 1 — turning a redox reaction into an electric current, and measuring electrode potentials.

nodes.label: Oxidation and reduction in separate half-cells

visual.alt: Flow: a spontaneous redox reaction split into two half-cells drives electrons through a wire to do work

slides.narration: Namaste! A torch cell, a mobile phone battery and the pacemaker in a patient’s chest all turn chemical energy into electrical energy. In this chapter we see how a redox reaction can be split into two halves so that electrons are forced to travel through a wire, how such a cell is written in shorthand, and how the tendency of each electrode to gain or lose electrons is measured.

slides.heading: Electrolytic and electrochemical cells
slides.body_md: In an **electrochemical (galvanic or voltaic) cell**, a spontaneous redox reaction produces electrical energy. In an **electrolytic cell**, electrical energy from an outside source drives a non-spontaneous reaction. In both, **oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode**.

visual.alt: Table comparing electrochemical and electrolytic cells

slides.narration: There are two kinds of cell. In an electrochemical, or galvanic, cell a spontaneous reaction pushes electrons through a wire, so chemical energy becomes electrical energy. In an electrolytic cell a battery forces a reaction that would not happen on its own. One rule holds in both: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Only the signs of the electrodes swap.

visual.caption: Zinc is the anode (oxidation, negative); copper is the cathode (reduction, positive).

slides.narration: Here is the Daniell cell. A zinc rod stands in zinc sulfate solution and a copper rod in copper sulfate solution. A wire joins the rods through a voltmeter, and a salt bridge joins the two solutions. With both solutions at one molar the voltmeter reads about one point one volts, and electrons flow through the wire from the zinc to the copper.

slides.heading: How the cell produces a current
slides.body_md: Zinc has a greater tendency to lose electrons than copper. Zinc atoms are **oxidised** at the anode; the electrons flow through the external wire to the copper, where Cu²⁺ ions are **reduced**. The **salt bridge** (KCl, KNO₃ or NH₄NO₃ in agar) lets ions migrate so that both solutions stay neutral, completing the circuit.

rows: Supplies ions to neutralise charge build-up
Cu²⁺ does not react directly with zinc

visual.alt: Table of the functions of a salt bridge

slides.narration: Why does current flow? Zinc gives up electrons more readily than copper. Zinc atoms lose two electrons each and enter the solution as zinc ions; the electrons travel through the wire to the copper rod, where copper ions pick them up and deposit as copper metal. Without the salt bridge, positive charge would pile up around the zinc and negative charge around the copper, and the current would stop almost at once.

slides.heading: Cell notation
slides.body_md: **Anode on the left, cathode on the right.** A single vertical line marks a phase boundary; a double line is the salt bridge. Concentrations (or pressures) are given in brackets. An inert electrode (Pt) is written at the end when the half-cell has no metal of its own.

rows: Inert electrode for gas or ion–ion half-cells

visual.alt: Table of conventions in cell notation

math: \ce{Pt | H2(g, 1 bar) | H+(aq, 1 M) || Ag+(aq, 1 M) | Ag(s)}
slides.narration: Cells are written in a shorthand. The anode goes on the left and the cathode on the right. A single line marks the boundary between a solid and a solution, and a double line stands for the salt bridge. When a half-cell involves a gas or two ions, an inert platinum electrode is written at the end. The cell voltage is the right-hand potential minus the left-hand one.

slides.heading: Worked example: from a reaction to cell notation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the half-reactions and the cell notation for a cell based on $\ce{Fe(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Fe^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)}$, with 0.1 M Fe²⁺ and 0.5 M Ag⁺.

**Step 1.** Oxidation (anode): $\ce{Fe -> Fe^2+ + 2e-}$; reduction (cathode): $\ce{Ag+ + e- -> Ag}$ (twice).

**Step 2.** $\ce{Fe(s) | Fe^2+(aq, 0.1 M) || Ag+(aq, 0.5 M) | Ag(s)}$.

visual.alt: Table of the iron and silver half-cells, their processes and positions

slides.narration: Start with the overall reaction and find which species loses electrons. Iron goes from zero to plus two, so it is oxidised: that half-cell is the anode and goes on the left. Silver ions gain electrons and are reduced at the cathode, written on the right. Put the concentrations in brackets and join the two halves with a double line for the salt bridge.

slides.heading: Quick check: anode or cathode?
slides.body_md: Identify the anode, or the direction of electron flow, from a cell notation.
slides.narration: Quick check. The left-hand electrode in cell notation is the anode, where oxidation takes place, and electrons leave it through the wire.

slides.heading: Single electrode potential
slides.body_md: When a metal dips into a solution of its ions, an equilibrium $\ce{M^{n+} + ne- <=> M}$ sets up and a potential difference develops between metal and solution: the **electrode potential**. Its absolute value **cannot be measured**; only differences between two electrodes can. So all potentials are measured against a reference, the **standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)**, assigned $E^\circ = 0.00\ \text{V}$ at all temperatures. By IUPAC convention potentials are quoted as **reduction potentials**.

rows: Potential difference between an electrode and its solution
Measured at 1 M ions, 1 bar gas, 298 K

visual.alt: Table of terms about electrode potential

slides.narration: When a metal is dipped into a solution of its own ions, some atoms may lose electrons and enter the solution, or some ions may gain electrons and deposit, until an equilibrium is reached. A potential difference builds up between the metal and the solution. We cannot measure this on its own, because any measuring wire forms a second electrode. So we measure every electrode against one agreed reference, the standard hydrogen electrode.

slides.heading: The standard hydrogen electrode
slides.body_md: **Preparation:** a platinum foil coated with **platinum black** (finely divided Pt, large surface; adsorbs H₂) dips into 1 M H⁺ (e.g. HCl) at 298 K; pure hydrogen gas at **1 bar** is bubbled over it. Half-reaction: $\ce{2H+(aq) + 2e- <=> H2(g)}$, $E^\circ = 0$. **Limitations:** hard to keep H⁺ exactly 1 M and H₂ exactly 1 bar; platinum is easily poisoned by impurities (e.g. arsenic, sulfur compounds); cannot be used in solutions of oxidising agents; inconvenient to set up, so secondary reference electrodes are used in practice.

slides.narration: This is the standard hydrogen electrode. A platinum foil coated with finely divided platinum black, which gives a large surface and adsorbs hydrogen, dips into acid with hydrogen ions at one mole per litre. Pure hydrogen at one bar bubbles over it. Its potential is defined as zero. But it is awkward: the acid concentration and gas pressure must be exact, platinum is easily poisoned, and it cannot be used with oxidising agents.

slides.heading: Measuring E° of Zn²⁺/Zn and Cu²⁺/Cu
slides.body_md: The half-cell is connected to the SHE through a salt bridge and a voltmeter. The **direction of electron flow** decides the sign.

visual.alt: Table showing how the signs of the zinc and copper standard potentials follow from electron flow

math: \ce{Zn | Zn^2+(1 M) || H+(1 M) | H2(1 bar) | Pt}: \ E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.76\ \text{V} = 0 - E^\circ_{\ce{Zn^2+/Zn}}
\ce{Pt | H2(1 bar) | H+(1 M) || Cu^2+(1 M) | Cu}: \ E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.34\ \text{V} = E^\circ_{\ce{Cu^2+/Cu}} - 0
slides.narration: To measure the standard potential of zinc, join a zinc half-cell with one molar zinc ions to the standard hydrogen electrode. Electrons flow from the zinc to the hydrogen electrode, so zinc is the anode, and the voltmeter reads nought point seven six volts; the reduction potential of zinc is therefore minus nought point seven six. With copper, electrons flow the other way, copper is the cathode, and its potential is plus nought point three four volts.

slides.heading: Worked example: finding an unknown standard potential
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A nickel half-cell (1 M Ni²⁺) is connected to the SHE. The voltmeter reads $0.25\ \text{V}$ and electrons flow from the nickel to the SHE. Find $E^\circ_{\ce{Ni^2+/Ni}}$ and write the cell.

**Step 1.** Electrons leave nickel, so nickel is the anode (left).

**Step 2.** $\ce{Ni | Ni^2+(1 M) || H+(1 M) | H2(1 bar) | Pt}$.

**Step 3.** $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0 - E^\circ_{\ce{Ni^2+/Ni}} = 0.25$, so $E^\circ_{\ce{Ni^2+/Ni}} = -0.25\ \text{V}$.

visual.alt: Flow for finding an unknown standard electrode potential against the SHE

slides.narration: The direction of electron flow tells us which electrode is the anode. Electrons leave the nickel, so nickel is oxidised and is the anode. The cell voltage, nought point two five, equals the cathode potential, zero for hydrogen, minus the nickel potential. So the standard reduction potential of nickel is minus nought point two five volts.

slides.body_md: Recall a feature or a limitation of the standard hydrogen electrode.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what makes the hydrogen electrode standard, and why chemists avoid it in everyday measurements.

slides.heading: Quick check: sign of E°
slides.body_md: Deduce the sign of a standard electrode potential from the direction of electron flow.
slides.narration: Quick check. If the half-cell is the anode when joined to the SHE, its reduction potential is negative.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Galvanic cell: spontaneous reaction → electricity; electrolytic cell: electricity drives reaction.
Oxidation at anode, reduction at cathode; salt bridge completes the circuit.
Cell notation: anode | anode solution || cathode solution | cathode.
Electrode potentials are measured against the SHE (E° = 0); quoted as reduction potentials.
SHE: Pt black, 1 M H⁺, H₂ at 1 bar; limitations: hard to maintain, poisoned, not with oxidants.

visual.alt: Summary table of four standard electrode potentials

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. A galvanic cell separates oxidation and reduction so that electrons flow through a wire; the salt bridge completes the circuit. Cells are written with the anode on the left. Electrode potentials are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, which has zero potential but is awkward to use. The direction of electron flow gives the sign of each potential.

Writing the cathode on the left
Taken as zero at all temperatures

Decide the sign of a standard potential from the direction of electron flow. And always write the half-reactions with state symbols.

decks.title: Electrochemical Cells and Electrode Potential — Part 2: Electrochemical series and the Nernst equation
goals: Predict how electrode potential changes with concentration, temperature and the nature of the electrode
Use the electrochemical series to predict displacement reactions and calculate standard cell emf
Calculate the emf of a cell at non-standard concentrations using the Nernst equation
Calculate ΔG° and the equilibrium constant from the standard cell emf

slides.heading: Electrode potentials at work
slides.body_md: Part 2 — ranking electrodes, predicting reactions and correcting for concentration.

visual.alt: Flow of topics in Part 2

slides.narration: Once we can measure electrode potentials, we can rank them in a series and use it to predict which metal will displace another, whether a metal will liberate hydrogen from an acid, and how large a cell’s voltage will be. The Nernst equation then tells us how the voltage changes when the solutions are not one molar, and links voltage to Gibbs energy and equilibrium.

slides.heading: Factors affecting electrode potential
slides.body_md: For $\ce{M^{n+} + ne- <=> M}$: **(1) Concentration of ions:** increasing [Mⁿ⁺] shifts the equilibrium right and makes the reduction potential **more positive** (Le Chatelier; Nernst). **(2) Temperature:** E changes with T (the Nernst factor 2.303RT/nF grows with T). **(3) Nature of the electrode:** metals that lose electrons easily (low ionisation enthalpy, high hydration enthalpy of the ion) have **more negative** reduction potentials.

visual.alt: Electrode potential of a copper electrode against the logarithm of copper ion concentration: a straight line rising with slope about 0.03 volt per tenfold increase, reaching 0.34 volt at 1 mol per litre
visual.caption: Slope = 0.059/n = 0.0295 V per tenfold change in concentration (n = 2).

slides.narration: Three things affect an electrode potential. First, concentration: adding more metal ions pushes the reduction equilibrium forward, so the potential becomes more positive; for copper it rises by about three hundredths of a volt for each tenfold increase. Second, temperature, because the Nernst factor contains temperature. Third, the nature of the metal itself: metals that give up electrons easily have very negative reduction potentials.

slides.heading: Quick check: factors affecting E
slides.body_md: Predict how an electrode potential changes when the ion concentration changes.
slides.narration: Quick check. More metal ions push the reduction equilibrium forward, making the potential more positive.

slides.heading: The electrochemical series
slides.body_md: Standard **reduction** potentials arranged in order. **More positive** $E^\circ$: stronger **oxidising agent**. **More negative** $E^\circ$: stronger **reducing agent**, more reactive metal.

visual.alt: Table of standard reduction potentials at 298 K from fluorine to potassium

slides.narration: Here is an electrochemical series written as reductions. Fluorine at the top, with the most positive value, grabs electrons most strongly: it is the strongest oxidising agent. Potassium near the bottom gives electrons away most readily: it is the strongest reducing agent and a very reactive metal. Notice that the iron three to iron two couple sits just below silver.

slides.heading: Worked example: standard emf and the cell reaction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{Al | Al^3+ (1 M) || Ni^2+ (1 M) | Ni}$, find $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ and write the balanced cell reaction. ($E^\circ$: Al³⁺/Al $-1.66$ V, Ni²⁺/Ni $-0.25$ V)

**Step 1.** $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode} = -0.25 - (-1.66) = 1.41\ \text{V}$.

**Step 2.** Electrons: Al gives 3, Ni²⁺ takes 2; LCM 6.

**Step 3.** $\ce{2Al(s) + 3Ni^2+(aq) -> 2Al^3+(aq) + 3Ni(s)}$; $n = 6$. $E^\circ$ is **not** multiplied by the coefficients.

visual.alt: Table of the aluminium–nickel cell with standard potentials and emf

slides.narration: Subtract the anode potential from the cathode potential: minus nought point two five minus minus one point six six gives one point four one volts. To balance the reaction, each aluminium atom gives three electrons and each nickel ion takes two, so we need two aluminium and three nickel, with six electrons in all. The potentials are not multiplied by these numbers, because electrode potential does not depend on the amount of substance.

slides.heading: Using the series to predict reactions
slides.body_md: (1) A metal with a **lower** (more negative) E° displaces a metal with a higher E° from a solution of its salt. (2) Metals with **negative** E° liberate H₂ from dilute acids; those with positive E° do not. (3) A reaction is feasible if the calculated $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ is **positive**.

rows: Does iron displace copper from CuSO₄?
Yes: E° of Fe (−0.44) is lower than Cu (+0.34)
Does silver liberate H₂ from dilute HCl?
No: E° of Ag is positive
Can Br₂ oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺?

visual.alt: Table of predictions from the electrochemical series

slides.narration: The series becomes a prediction tool. A metal lower in the list displaces one higher up, so iron displaces copper. Metals with negative potentials release hydrogen from dilute acids; copper and silver do not. For any redox reaction, imagine it happens, calculate the cell voltage, and if the answer is positive the reaction is feasible: bromine can oxidise iron two ions, but iodine cannot.

slides.heading: Worked example: storing a solution
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Can a copper(II) sulfate solution be stored in an iron tank? Can it be stored in a silver vessel? ($E^\circ$: Cu²⁺/Cu $+0.34$, Fe²⁺/Fe $-0.44$, Ag⁺/Ag $+0.80$ V)

**Iron tank:** $\ce{Fe + Cu^2+ -> Fe^2+ + Cu}$: $E^\circ = 0.34 - (-0.44) = 0.78\ \text{V}$, positive — the tank would dissolve. **No.**

**Silver vessel:** $\ce{2Ag + Cu^2+ -> 2Ag+ + Cu}$: $E^\circ = 0.34 - 0.80 = -0.46\ \text{V}$, negative — no reaction. **Yes.**

visual.alt: Table of the two storage tests with cell emf and verdict

slides.narration: For each vessel, imagine the metal reacting with copper ions. With iron, the cell voltage is nought point three four minus minus nought point four four, a positive nought point seven eight volts, so iron would dissolve and copper would deposit. With silver, the voltage is nought point three four minus nought point eight, which is negative, so nothing happens and the silver vessel is safe.

slides.heading: Quick check: electrochemical series
slides.body_md: Use standard reduction potentials to choose the strongest oxidising or reducing agent, or to predict a displacement.
slides.narration: Quick check. More positive potential, stronger oxidising agent; more negative, stronger reducing agent.

slides.heading: The Nernst equation
slides.body_md: For an electrode $\ce{M^{n+} + ne- -> M}$ and for a cell reaction with reaction quotient $Q$ (pure solids omitted), at temperature $T$ and, numerically, at $298\ \text{K}$:

visual.alt: Table of the symbols in the Nernst equation

slides.narration: Real solutions are rarely exactly one molar, so Nernst gave an equation to correct the standard potential. For a whole cell, the voltage equals the standard voltage minus nought point nought five nine over n, times the logarithm of the reaction quotient, at twenty five degrees Celsius. The quotient is products over reactants, using concentrations of ions and leaving out pure solids.

slides.heading: Worked example: emf at non-standard concentrations

visual.alt: Table of values in the nickel–copper Nernst example

slides.narration: First find the standard voltage, nought point five nine volts, with two electrons transferred. The reaction quotient is the product ion, nickel, over the reactant ion, copper: nought point nought one over nought point one, which is a tenth, with a logarithm of minus one. Subtracting a negative term raises the voltage slightly, to about nought point six two volts.

slides.heading: Emf, Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant
slides.body_md: The maximum electrical work a cell can do equals the decrease in Gibbs energy. A **positive** $E_\text{cell}$ means **negative** $\Delta G$: spontaneous. At equilibrium $E_\text{cell} = 0$ and $Q = K$.

visual.alt: Table linking E°cell, ΔG° and K

slides.narration: A cell can do electrical work equal to the fall in its Gibbs energy, so the Gibbs energy change equals minus n F times the voltage. A positive voltage means a negative Gibbs energy change and a spontaneous reaction. When the cell is flat it is at equilibrium: the voltage is zero and the quotient equals the equilibrium constant, which gives a direct link between the standard voltage and K.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔG° and K from E°
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{Cu(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Cu^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)}$, $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.46\ \text{V}$. Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ at $298\ \text{K}$ ($F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$).

**Step 1.** $n = 2$; $\Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.46 = -88780\ \text{J} = -88.78\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $\log K = \dfrac{2 \times 0.46}{0.059} = 15.59$.

**Step 3.** $K = 10^{15.59} \approx 3.9 \times 10^{15}$.

visual.alt: Table of the Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant for the copper–silver cell

slides.narration: Two electrons are transferred. Minus two times ninety six thousand five hundred times nought point four six gives about minus eighty nine kilojoules per mole, a clearly spontaneous reaction. For the equilibrium constant, two times nought point four six over nought point nought five nine is about fifteen point six, so K is about four times ten to the fifteen: copper reduces silver ions almost completely.

slides.heading: Quick check: Nernst and ΔG
slides.body_md: Predict how the emf changes with concentration, or link the sign of E° to ΔG° and K.
slides.narration: Quick check. Increasing the reactant ion concentration lowers Q and raises the emf. A positive standard emf means a negative standard Gibbs energy change and an equilibrium constant greater than one.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: E depends on ion concentration, temperature and the nature of the electrode.
Electrochemical series: more positive E°, stronger oxidant; more negative, stronger reductant.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Electrode potentials depend on concentration, temperature and the metal. sections.heading: 1. Electrolytic and electrochemical cells; the Daniell cell
sections.body_md:
**Electrochemical (galvanic/voltaic) cell:** spontaneous redox reaction → electrical energy; anode negative, cathode positive. **Electrolytic cell:** electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction; anode positive, cathode negative. In both, oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode.

**Daniell cell:** $\ce{Zn(s) + Cu^2+(aq) -> Zn^2+(aq) + Cu(s)}$; anode $\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$, cathode $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$; $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.10\ \text{V}$. Electrons flow in the external circuit from Zn to Cu; current flows from Cu to Zn.

**Salt bridge** (KCl, KNO₃ or NH₄NO₃ in agar): completes the circuit, maintains electrical neutrality, prevents mixing of solutions, minimises liquid junction potential.

**Cell notation:** anode | anode electrolyte || cathode electrolyte | cathode; $E_\text{cell} = E_\text{right} - E_\text{left}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction produces electrical energy.
A tube of an inert electrolyte in agar that connects the two half-cells and keeps them electrically neutral.
The electrode at which oxidation occurs.

sections.heading: 2. Single electrode potential and the SHE
sections.body_md:
An electrode in contact with its ions sets up $\ce{M^{n+} + ne- <=> M}$; the resulting potential difference is the **electrode potential**. Absolute values cannot be measured, so potentials are measured against the **standard hydrogen electrode** (E° = 0 V at all temperatures) and quoted as **reduction potentials** (IUPAC). Standard conditions: 1 M ions, 1 bar gases, 298 K.

**SHE:** Pt foil coated with platinum black in 1 M H⁺, pure H₂ at 1 bar bubbled over it; $\ce{2H+(aq) + 2e- <=> H2(g)}$. **Limitations:** difficult to maintain exactly 1 M H⁺ and 1 bar H₂; Pt easily poisoned; cannot be used in the presence of oxidising agents; cumbersome.

**Measuring E°:** Zn | Zn²⁺(1 M) || SHE gives 0.76 V with Zn as anode, so $E^\circ_{\ce{Zn^2+/Zn}} = -0.76\ \text{V}$; SHE || Cu²⁺(1 M) | Cu gives 0.34 V with Cu as cathode, so $E^\circ_{\ce{Cu^2+/Cu}} = +0.34\ \text{V}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The reduction potential of an electrode measured against the SHE with 1 M ions, 1 bar gases at 298 K.
A reference electrode of platinised platinum in 1 M H⁺ with H₂ at 1 bar, assigned zero potential.

sections.heading: 3. Factors affecting electrode potential
sections.body_md:
- **Concentration of ions:** for $\ce{M^{n+} + ne- -> M}$, $E = E^\circ + \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log[\ce{M^{n+}}]$ at 298 K; higher [Mⁿ⁺] gives a more positive E.
- **Temperature:** the Nernst factor $2.303RT/nF$ increases with $T$.
- **Nature of the electrode:** metals with low sublimation and ionisation enthalpies and high hydration enthalpy of their ions lose electrons easily and have more negative E°.

key_terms.definition_md: The potential difference between an electrode and the solution of its ions.

visual.caption: Slope = 0.059/n = 0.0295 V per tenfold change in concentration (n = 2).

sections.heading: 4. Electrochemical series
sections.body_md:
Electrodes arranged in order of standard reduction potential (F₂/F⁻ +2.87 … Li⁺/Li −3.05 V).

**Applications:** (1) relative strengths of oxidising and reducing agents (more positive E° → stronger oxidant); (2) a metal with lower E° displaces one with higher E° from its salt solution; (3) metals with negative E° liberate H₂ from dilute acids; (4) $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode}$; (5) feasibility: a redox reaction is spontaneous if $E^\circ_\text{cell} > 0$.

E° is an **intensive** property: it is not multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients.

key_terms.definition_md: The arrangement of electrodes in order of their standard reduction potentials.

sections.heading: 5. Nernst equation, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant
sections.body_md:
**Nernst equation:** $E_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{2.303RT}{nF}\log Q = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q$ (298 K); $Q$ = products ÷ reactants, pure solids omitted. For the hydrogen electrode, $E = -0.059\,\text{pH}$ (1 bar H₂).

**Gibbs energy:** $\Delta G = -nFE_\text{cell}$, $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$; spontaneous if $E > 0$ ($\Delta G < 0$).

**Equilibrium constant:** at equilibrium $E_\text{cell} = 0$, so $E^\circ_\text{cell} = \dfrac{2.303RT}{nF}\log K = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K$ (298 K); also $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$.

The charge on one mole of electrons, about 96500 C mol⁻¹.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the anode positive in a galvanic cell.
- Multiplying E° by stoichiometric coefficients.
- Writing Q as reactants over products, or including pure solids.
- Forgetting the minus sign in ΔG° = −nFE°, or leaving ΔG° in joules when kJ is asked.
- Getting the sign of E° wrong when a half-cell is measured against the SHE.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Cell questions: half-reactions with states, cell notation, emf with sign.
- Nernst numericals: correct Q, n and log value, substitution, answer with units.
- SHE: diagram or description (Pt black, 1 M H⁺, 1 bar H₂) and limitations.

questions.stem_md: In the cell $\ce{Pb(s) | Pb^2+(aq) || Ag+(aq) | Ag(s)}$, electrons in the external wire flow:

options.text_md: from the lead electrode to the silver electrode
from the silver electrode to the lead electrode
through the salt bridge from lead to silver

questions.solution_md: The left electrode (Pb) is the anode; electrons leave the anode through the wire to the cathode (Ag) — option (a). Ions, not electrons, move in the salt bridge (c).

options.text_md: The anode is the positive electrode
Chemical energy is converted into electrical energy

questions.solution_md: In an electrolytic cell the anode is joined to the positive terminal of the supply — option (a). Oxidation at the anode is true of both (b).

options.text_md: nitrate ions conduct electricity faster than any other ion
chloride ions would precipitate silver chloride
potassium chloride is insoluble in agar
nitrate ions take part in the cell reaction

questions.solution_md: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) would block the junction and remove Ag⁺ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For the cell $\ce{Mg(s) | Mg^2+(aq) || Cu^2+(aq) | Cu(s)}$, the reaction at the cathode is:
questions.solution_md: The right-hand electrode is the cathode, where reduction of Cu²⁺ occurs — option (b). Oxidation of Mg (a) happens at the anode.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a galvanic cell, the electrode at which oxidation takes place is the positive electrode.
questions.solution_md: False. In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode, which is the negative electrode.

**Reason (R):** The salt bridge allows ions to migrate so that both half-cells remain electrically neutral.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: without it, charge builds up and the circuit is broken — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between an electrochemical (galvanic) cell and an electrolytic cell.

answer.model_answer_md: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy using a spontaneous reaction, while an electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode positive; in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode negative.

questions.solution_md: Energy conversion; polarity.

questions.stem_md: For the reaction $\ce{Zn(s) + 2Fe^3+(aq) -> Zn^2+(aq) + 2Fe^2+(aq)}$, write the anode and cathode half-reactions and the cell notation (use platinum for the iron half-cell).

Anode: $\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$. Cathode: $\ce{Fe^3+ + e- -> Fe^2+}$ (twice).

questions.stem_md: Describe how a Daniell cell produces an electric current. Write the half-reactions and state two functions of the salt bridge.

answer.model_answer_md: A zinc rod in zinc sulfate solution is joined by a wire and a salt bridge to a copper rod in copper sulfate solution. Zinc loses electrons more readily than copper: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode. The electrons travel through the wire to the copper, where Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu at the cathode, so a current flows. The salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral (it also prevents the solutions from mixing).

questions.stem_md: Explain, with cell notations, how the standard electrode potentials of Zn²⁺/Zn and Cu²⁺/Cu are measured using the standard hydrogen electrode, and how their signs are decided.

answer.model_answer_md: Each half-cell (1 M ions, 298 K) is joined to the SHE through a salt bridge and a voltmeter. For zinc, electrons flow from Zn to the SHE, so zinc is the anode: $\ce{Zn | Zn^2+(1 M) || H+(1 M) | H2(1 bar) | Pt}$; $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.76 = 0 - E^\circ_{\ce{Zn^2+/Zn}}$, so $E^\circ = -0.76\ \text{V}$. questions.stem_md: Calculate the electrode potential, in V, of a silver electrode dipped in $0.010\ \text{M}$ silver nitrate at $298\ \text{K}$. ($E^\circ_{\ce{Ag+/Ag}} = +0.80\ \text{V}$)
State three factors on which the electrode potential of a metal dipped in a solution of its ions depends.

answer.model_answer_md: The concentration of the metal ions in solution (higher concentration, more positive reduction potential), the temperature, and the nature of the metal (its ionisation enthalpy, sublimation enthalpy and the hydration enthalpy of its ion).

questions.solution_md: Concentration, temperature, nature.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the reduction potential at 298 K of (a) a zinc electrode in 0.001 M Zn²⁺ and (b) a copper electrode in 0.1 M Cu²⁺. (E°: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V) (c) Hence find the emf of the cell made from these two electrodes.
Standard reduction potentials (V): Br₂/Br⁻ +1.09, I₂/I⁻ +0.54, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77, Sn⁴⁺/Sn²⁺ +0.15. Which is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.solution_md: The reduced form of the couple with the lowest E° is the strongest reducing agent — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Given E° (V): Al³⁺/Al −1.66, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44, Pb²⁺/Pb −0.13, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34. Which metal can displace lead from lead nitrate solution but cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate?
questions.solution_md: Iron (−0.44) lies below lead (−0.13) but above zinc (−0.76) — option (b). Aluminium displaces both (c); copper displaces neither (a).

questions.stem_md: Which metal will NOT liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.solution_md: Only metals with negative E° reduce H⁺ to H₂ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: E°(Cr³⁺/Cr) = −0.74 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. The standard emf of the cell Cr | Cr³⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag is:
questions.solution_md: E° = 0.80 − (−0.74) = 1.54 V; E° is not multiplied by 3 (c) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which halogen can oxidise both Br⁻ and I⁻ ions but not F⁻? (E°/V: F₂ 2.87, Cl₂ 1.36, Br₂ 1.09, I₂ 0.54)
questions.solution_md: Cl₂ has a higher E° than Br₂ and I₂ but lower than F₂ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Using the electrochemical series, match each observation with its explanation.

options.text_md: Zinc dissolves in dilute HCl, releasing H₂
Copper does not react with dilute HCl
Iron displaces copper from CuSO₄ solution
Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent

match_right.text_md: E° of Fe is lower than that of Cu

questions.solution_md: Each observation follows from the position of the couple in the series.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The standard potential of 2Cu²⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2Cu is twice that of Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

**Reason (R):** Electrode potential is an intensive property.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false — both have E° = +0.34 V; R is true and is the reason the value is unchanged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A metal higher in the electrochemical series (more positive E°) displaces a metal lower in the series from its salt solution.
questions.solution_md: False. The metal with the lower (more negative) E° displaces the one with the higher E°.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the standard emf, in V, of the cell $\ce{Al(s) | Al^3+(1 M) || Cu^2+(1 M) | Cu(s)}$. ($E^\circ$: Al³⁺/Al $-1.66$ V, Cu²⁺/Cu $+0.34$ V)
questions.solution_md: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode} = 0.34 - (-1.66) = 2.00$, so $2.00\ \text{V}$.

questions.stem_md: Predict, with calculation, whether iodine can oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ under standard conditions. (E°: I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V)

answer.model_answer_md: Assume $\ce{2Fe^2+ + I2 -> 2Fe^3+ + 2I-}$: cathode I₂/I⁻, anode Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺. $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.54 - 0.77 = -0.23\ \text{V}$. Negative, so the reaction is not feasible: iodine cannot oxidise Fe²⁺ (instead Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻).

questions.solution_md: −0.23 V, not feasible.

questions.stem_md: Can a solution of nickel(II) sulfate be stirred with a copper rod, and can it be stored in a zinc container? Justify each answer. (E°: Ni²⁺/Ni −0.25 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V)

answer.model_answer_md: Copper rod: Cu + Ni²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Ni would have E° = −0.25 − 0.34 = −0.59 V, negative, so there is no reaction and the copper rod can be used. Zinc container: Zn + Ni²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Ni has E° = −0.25 − (−0.76) = +0.51 V, positive, so zinc would dissolve; it cannot be used.

questions.solution_md: Copper yes; zinc no.

questions.stem_md: State three applications of the electrochemical series, illustrating each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Comparing oxidising and reducing strength: F₂, with the highest E°, is the strongest oxidising agent; Li, with the lowest, is the strongest reducing agent. (2) Predicting displacement: zinc (E° −0.76 V) displaces copper (+0.34 V) from copper sulfate solution. (3) Predicting reaction with acids: metals with negative E°, such as magnesium, liberate H₂ from dilute acids, while copper does not. (Also: calculating E°cell and predicting feasibility.)

questions.solution_md: Three applications with examples.

questions.stem_md: A cell is made from a magnesium electrode in 1 M Mg²⁺ and a lead electrode in 1 M Pb²⁺. (E°: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V, Pb²⁺/Pb −0.13 V) (a) Which electrode is the anode? (b) Write the cell notation and the cell reaction. (c) Calculate E°cell.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Magnesium (lower E°) is the anode.

(b) $\ce{Mg(s) | Mg^2+(1 M) || Pb^2+(1 M) | Pb(s)}$; $\ce{Mg(s) + Pb^2+(aq) -> Mg^2+(aq) + Pb(s)}$.

(c) $E^\circ_\text{cell} = -0.13 - (-2.37) = 2.24\ \text{V}$.

questions.solution_md: Mg anode; 2.24 V.

questions.stem_md: For the cell $\ce{Zn | Zn^2+(c_1) || Cu^2+(c_2) | Cu}$, which change increases the emf at 298 K?
questions.solution_md: E = E° − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); raising [Cu²⁺] lowers Q and raises E — option (c). The size of the electrode has no effect (b).

questions.stem_md: A concentration cell Cu | Cu²⁺(0.01 M) || Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu is set up at 298 K. Its emf is about:
For a cell reaction with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.40 V at 298 K, ΔG° is about (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹):
A two-electron cell reaction has E°cell = 0.059 V at 298 K. Its equilibrium constant is:
A torch cell has run until it no longer gives any current. At this stage:

options.text_md: Ecell = 0 and the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant

questions.solution_md: A flat cell is at equilibrium: E = 0 and Q = K; E° and ΔG° are fixed constants — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A hydrogen electrode (H₂ at 1 bar) dips into a solution and shows a potential of −0.236 V at 298 K. The pH of the solution is:
At 298 K, the value of 2.303RT/F in the Nernst equation is ___ V.
True or false? A cell reaction with a positive standard emf has an equilibrium constant greater than 1.
questions.solution_md: True. log K = nE°/0.059 is positive, so K > 1.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A cell reaction with a negative standard emf has a positive standard Gibbs energy change.

**Reason (R):** ΔG° = −nFE°cell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the minus sign in R makes ΔG° positive when E° is negative — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A magnesium–copper cell is set up with 0.001 M Mg²⁺ and 0.0001 M Cu²⁺ at 298 K. Its standard emf is 2.71 V. What is the emf of the cell, in volts, under these conditions?
For the cell reaction $\ce{2Al(s) + 3Ni^2+(aq) -> 2Al^3+(aq) + 3Ni(s)}$, $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.41\ \text{V}$. Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$ in kJ mol⁻¹ ($F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$).
Calculate $\log K$ at $298\ \text{K}$ for $\ce{Fe(s) + Cu^2+(aq) -> Fe^2+(aq) + Cu(s)}$, given $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.78\ \text{V}$.
Write the Nernst equation for the cell Fe | Fe²⁺(aq) || Ag⁺(aq) | Ag at 298 K, and state how its emf changes if [Ag⁺] is increased.

answer.model_answer_md: Cell reaction $\ce{Fe + 2Ag+ -> Fe^2+ + 2Ag}$, $n = 2$: $E_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\ce{Fe^2+}]}{[\ce{Ag+}]^2}$. Increasing [Ag⁺] decreases Q, so the emf increases.

questions.solution_md: Equation with [Ag⁺]²; emf rises.

marking_scheme.step: Correct Nernst equation with squared term

questions.stem_md: Show how the standard emf of a cell is related to its equilibrium constant at 298 K, starting from the Nernst equation.

answer.model_answer_md: $E_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q$. At equilibrium $E_\text{cell} = 0$ and $Q = K$, so $0 = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K$, giving $E^\circ_\text{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K$.

questions.solution_md: E = 0, Q = K at equilibrium.

marking_scheme.step: E = 0 and Q = K at equilibrium

questions.stem_md: For the cell Cu(s) | Cu²⁺(0.02 M) || Ag⁺(0.2 M) | Ag(s) at 298 K (E°: Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V): (a) write the cell reaction, (b) calculate E°cell and (c) calculate Ecell.
For the cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(1 M) || Ag⁺(1 M) | Ag(s) at 298 K (E°: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V), calculate (a) E°cell, (b) ΔG° and (c) log K. (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)

A cell is made of a hydrogen electrode (H₂ at 1 bar) dipping into a solution of unknown pH, connected to the SHE. The emf at 298 K is 0.354 V. (a) Which electrode is the anode? (b) Calculate the pH of the solution. (c) Would the emf rise or fall if the solution were made more acidic?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The electrode in the unknown solution has the lower [H⁺], so its potential is negative ($E = -0.059\,\text{pH}$); it is the anode.

(b) $E_\text{cell} = 0 - (-0.059\,\text{pH}) = 0.059\,\text{pH} = 0.354$, so $\text{pH} = 6.0$.

(c) A more acidic solution has a lower pH, so the emf would fall (towards zero at pH 0).

questions.solution_md: Unknown electrode anode; pH 6.0; emf falls.

(a) Derive the relation between the standard emf of a cell and the equilibrium constant of its reaction, starting from ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −2.303RT log K. [2]

(b) For the cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(0.04 M) || Ni²⁺(0.4 M) | Ni(s) at 298 K (E°: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Ni²⁺/Ni −0.25 V), calculate (i) E°cell, (ii) Ecell and (iii) ΔG° (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹). [3]
questions.solution_md: Derivation; 0.51 V; 0.540 V; −98.43 kJ/mol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is the electrochemical series? How does it help to predict whether a metal will liberate hydrogen from a dilute acid? [2]

(b) Given E° (V): Ag⁺/Ag +0.80, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44, Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37: (i) which metal is the strongest reducing agent? (ii) Which pair of electrodes gives a cell of the highest standard emf, and what is its value? (iii) Will copper displace silver from silver nitrate solution? Justify. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The arrangement of electrodes (half-cells) in order of their standard reduction potentials. A metal with a negative E° is a stronger reducing agent than hydrogen and reduces H⁺ to H₂, so it liberates hydrogen from dilute acids; a metal with a positive E° does not. (b) (i) Magnesium (lowest E°). (ii) Mg and Ag: E°cell = 0.80 − (−2.37) = 3.17 V. (iii) Yes: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag has E°cell = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V, which is positive, so copper displaces silver.

questions.solution_md: Series; Mg; 3.17 V; yes (+0.46 V).

questions.stem_md:
(a) With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the construction and working of a Daniell cell. Write the reactions at each electrode and the cell notation. [3]

(b) Explain what happens to the emf of a Daniell cell as it is used, with reference to the Nernst equation. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A zinc rod dips into ZnSO₄ solution and a copper rod into CuSO₄ solution in separate beakers; the solutions are joined by a salt bridge and the rods by a wire through a voltmeter. Anode: $\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$; cathode: $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$; electrons flow from Zn to Cu through the wire. Notation: $\ce{Zn(s) | Zn^2+(aq) || Cu^2+(aq) | Cu(s)}$; $E^\circ = 1.10\ \text{V}$.

(b) $E = 1.10 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\ce{Zn^2+}]}{[\ce{Cu^2+}]}$. As the cell works, [Zn²⁺] rises and [Cu²⁺] falls, so Q increases and the emf falls, reaching zero when the reaction reaches equilibrium.

questions.solution_md: Construction and reactions; emf falls as Q rises.
